title: On Manipulating Signals of User-Item Graph: A Jacobi Polynomial-based Graph Collaborative Filtering

problem.claim: Graph collaborative filtering must determine which signal components contribute to recommendations and how to use them effectively.

gap.claim: Existing research lacks a study of how different signal components contribute to recommendations and how to properly use them.

contributions.claim: The authors analyze, from a spectral-transformation perspective, factors that graph filters should consider for better recommendation performance.
The authors design JGCF, an efficient and effective collaborative-filtering method based on Jacobi polynomial bases and frequency-decomposition strategies.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on four widely used public datasets are reported to show the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed methods.
The authors report an at-most 27.06% performance gain on Alibaba-iFashion.
The authors report that JGCF is better at handling sparse datasets, suggesting potential for recommendations to cold-start users.

narrative_sequence.summary: Collaborative filtering recommends items from user-item interaction information, and graph CF uses high-order information in the user-item bipartite graph.
Recent studies attribute the success of GNN-based collaborative filtering to low-pass filtering effects.
Research has not established how different signal components contribute to recommendations or how to use them properly.
The authors analyze graph-filter factors through spectral transformation and design JGCF using Jacobi polynomial bases and frequency decomposition.
Experiments report effectiveness, efficiency, gains on Alibaba-iFashion, and stronger handling of sparse datasets.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links graph collaborative-filtering performance to the treatment of signal components and graph-filter frequency behavior.

interpretation.claim: Analyzing signal components spectrally may help guide graph-filter design for recommendation tasks.

application.claim: For graph-based recommendation systems, evaluate and design filters with explicit attention to frequency decomposition and signal components.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach generalizes beyond the reported datasets or recommendation setting.

unknowns: The specific signal components, spectral factors, and frequency-decomposition details are not provided.
The four datasets, evaluation metrics, baselines, and experimental settings are not specified.
The abstract does not provide independent verification of the reported performance gains or cold-start potential.
